Whether demand was made could affect evaluation of the disputed contractual payment mechanism. The allowed excerpts do not establish a separate express finding resolving this factual issue.

source_evidence.quote: (a)by efflux of the time limited thereby;
(b)where such time is limited conditionally on the happening of some event—by the happening of such event;

serious_errors.materiality: Adds an incorrect statutory ground to Section 111(b), potentially confusing the contractual-event analysis with ordinary expiry of a fixed term. The statutory error is established, but its seriousness for the report's ultimate assessment is uncertain because the report also correctly describes the conditional-event aspect and the trial court's historical position.

important_omissions: The report does not explain that the 1913 defendants had already raised a no-notice objection which was rejected, even though relief against forfeiture was granted. This matters to the history of the recurring notice dispute.

The 1870 purchaser executed a separate rent note requiring payment in the month of Poush every year and declaring cessation of rights on default. The report mentions the rent note but omits its annual payment timing and distinct contractual undertaking.
In the present suit Defendant No. 1 asserted that Survey No. 86/2 had fallen to his share through partition. The report omits this specific property-right claim.

In the 1938 litigation Defendant No. 1 argued that no rent was fixed for the suit property and that the landlord bore responsibility for collection. The report discusses the broader payment-mechanism position but omits the historically rejected no-fixed-rent argument.

The report does not clearly distinguish the original 1941 possession claim concerning both Survey Nos. 86/1 and 86/2 from the restricted property scope of the later Supreme Court appeal. It states both property scopes in different contexts but does not explicitly connect the change.

The report omits the material procedural details of the possession decree: the trial court allowed Defendant No. 1 to retain two structures on Survey No. 86/2 until March 1950; the District appellate court permitted removal of buildings and trees; the plaintiff filed High Court cross-objections concerning trees and costs; and the High Court allowed those cross-objections.

The report does not distinguish the effects of the first appellate modifications, the High Court's second-appeal ruling, and the subsequent Supreme Court appeal beyond a general procedural sequence. This limits its explanation of the appeals and available remedies.

The report omits the recorded 1943 transfer of possession of the suit lands to the plaintiff, subject to the retained structures on Survey No. 86/2. This limits the account of the procedural posture and practical possession rights.
The appellant's express allegation that he offered rent and the landlord fraudulently refused it is not correctly reconstructed. The report instead reverses the parties to that allegation.

The report does not address the express relief conditions in Section 114, including arrears, interest, full suit costs or court-approved security, when discussing discretionary relief. The available record does not establish that these conditions were fulfilled in the present proceeding.

The report does not separately analyze the preservation of pre-Act rights and liabilities under Section 2(c) of the Transfer of Property Act or the possible agricultural-lease limitation in Section 117. Their applicability and consequences remain unresolved on the allowed view; the omissions do not justify assuming either provision controls.

The original lease premium of Rs. 999 and the Rs. 7,999 consideration for the 1870 transfer are omitted. They provide additional historical consideration for the permanent tenancy but their precise amounts are not shown to be necessary to the appellate questions.

The report does not explicitly identify the need to assess the separate legal consequences of historical waivers and prior equitable relief against the January 1941 default. Prior waivers and relief do not by themselves establish that the present forfeiture was waived or that further relief had to be granted.
main_answer_reason: The report supplies a substantial, source-grounded reconstruction of the competing notice positions, the trial and intermediate appellate classifications under Sections 111(b) and 111(g), the permanent lease and rent terms, historical defaults and waivers, the restriction of the present appeal to Survey No. 86/2, and the prior courts' discretionary refusal of relief. It generally attributes historical judicial views rather than expressly claiming to know the withheld target disposition. However, three confirmed material mistakes impair reliability: the original-to-modern property mapping is wrong; Defendant No. 1's fraudulent-refusal allegation is assigned to the plaintiff; and the High Court's standard for second-appeal interference is inverted. The report also presents a disputed rent demand without attribution, adds efflux of time to Section 111(b), and leaves important appellate modifications and legal conditions unexplained. These errors materially affect property identity, competing payment evidence and appellate review, but do not erase the substantial supported treatment of the principal dispute. PARTIAL best reflects the mixture without treating every unsupported formulation as a demonstrated incorrect ultimate conclusion.
uncertainties: The target appellate court's reasons and disposition are withheld. No assertion in this annotation treats the historical High Court findings as the target court's final endorsement.

The full legal effect of the 1863 lease under the pre-Act savings provisions, Section 111(g), and any relevant territorial or agricultural-lease limitations is not resolved by the supplied excerpts alone.

Whether the January 1941 rent was actually demanded and validly tendered remains disputed in the expressly reproduced party pleadings. The general statement that the trial court rejected the defences does not provide a separately reasoned resolution of each underlying allegation.

Source S711fe9f5bf05 describes Defendant No. 1 as having attained majority and taken charge in 1922–23, whereas source Sb7af28402465 states that he became a major in or about 1925. The report accurately attributes the former to the trial court, but the historical date discrepancy cannot be resolved from this view.

The report's 'two appeals' heading does not specify which pair of appellate proceedings is intended. The record contains a District appeal, a High Court second appeal and a later Supreme Court civil appeal.
The description of the landlord's compensated rights as 'reversionary interest' may be a permissible legal characterization, but the source itself says 'rights as landlord'.
The report's 'estoppel-like' characterization does not establish statutory estoppel, but its tentative wording does not necessarily assert that an actual estoppel ruling was made.

The ultimate correctness of the trial court's Section 111(b) analysis, the District appellate court's Section 111(g) analysis, and the historical denial of discretionary relief cannot be established by treating those reviewable findings as final law.
No conclusion about the relative performance of any anonymous method or any hidden judgment outcome is made.
